title: Walls that speak
text: For most of the twentieth century, the large painting on a public wall was a government's {{1}}: the mosaics of the Soviet metro, the works-progress murals of Depression America, the slogans of every revolutionary regime. Since then the wall has been {{2}} by the street. The shift is usually dated to graffiti writers in Philadelphia and New York in the 1970s, whose painted names treated the city as a {{3}} — vandalism, the authorities called it, and mostly it was. But the skills those writers developed {{4}} somewhere unexpected: commissioned murals, community projects and, eventually, museum walls. Today a mural {{5}} a double role: art in the open air, and a claim about who a neighbourhood belongs to. Cities have learned to {{6}} the difference between blight and brightness, and the best programmes pair writers with residents so that the walls answer to the people who {{7}} them. The economics favour the form, too: a mural costs almost {{8}}, needs no building, reaches everyone who walks past, and disappears — legally or otherwise — the way public art always has.

gaps.explanation: 'a government's instrument' — a means of achieving its aims; inscription = words carved on stone.
'the wall has been reclaimed by the street' — taken back by ordinary people; proclaim = announce publicly.
'treated the city as a canvas' — the painter's cloth, used figuratively; canon = an accepted list of works.
'the skills surfaced somewhere unexpected' — appeared publicly; surpass = excel.
'a mural plays a double role' — 'play a role' is the fixed phrase; ply = travel a route regularly, plod = walk heavily.
'learned to distinguish the difference between blight and brightness' — perceive it; extinguish = put out a fire.
'the people who inhabit them' — live in the neighbourhood; inhibit = hold back, inherit = receive from the past.
'costs almost nothing' — the only word that fits 'almost' when the point is that murals are cheap.
